shouldFix.title: The claim cell drops 'future' from v5's DR-131 pack limb, so an adopted register cell recites the pack as a present component of the useful install
shouldFix.finding: v5's EE-7a invariant reads 'Default useful install is signed distribution core + semantic host + one selected TypeScript closure + future DR-131 pack.' The proposed claim reads 'Preview useful-install selection is signed distribution core + semantic host + one TypeScript closure + DR-131 pack'. The word future is gone. DR-131's own live row is still a hard blocker for preview analyze, so the pack does not exist yet, and this cell would land permanently in file 08 as the gate's Claim.
shouldFix.whyItMatters: The draft's header expressly refuses to invent the DR-131 pack, and the review prompt lists inventing it as an attack, so the intent is not in doubt — the operative bytes just do not match the intent. The drafter was careful about this everywhere else: the evidence cell requires the TypeScript closure and never requires the pack, and v5's own EE-7a input tests only core-only advertisement and closure omission. That asymmetry is what convinces me the claim cell is a slip rather than a position: the one place the pack appears unqualified is the one place the qualifier was needed.
shouldFix.howItFails: A later reader cites the adopted DR-G30 Claim as evidence that the DR-131 pack is a committed present component of the preview useful install, while DR-131 remains an open hard blocker. Alternatively a harness author builds to the claim and produces a gate that cannot pass until an unbuilt pack ships.
shouldFix.whyNotMustFix: Membership of the pack in the selection is something v5 asserts too; only the temporal qualifier is lost, and the evidence cell — which governs what must be retained — excludes the pack entirely. So the cell is imprecise rather than false. I record that Codex may reasonably grade this MUST-FIX, as happened at D-140 and again at D-157 where its harder grade was the better call.
shouldFix.repair: Restore v5's word: '... + one TypeScript closure + future DR-131 pack'. Nothing else in the row needs to change.

coordinatorSummary: OBJECT at 0 MUST-FIX and 1 SHOULD-FIX. Fifteen attacks run, one landed, and the repair is a single word. Everything mechanical is clean. Custody holds: subject 1c03d11b at 0444 unmoved, HEAD never left 98e2e8b, governing tree clean, no D-158 heading, C-D158 unused, all five cited files reproduce and the D-157 commit is HEAD. I verified D-157's write rather than assuming it: the live table is 29 rows through DR-G29 with the condition-4 cell reading 29 of 29 owners and 25 of 25 required, exactly D-157's After operand. This draft's Before operand occurs exactly once in that live cell, all three fenced blocks are backslash-free, the row has 8 fields in header order, the segment diff of Before against After shows exactly four changes and no fifth, and the insertion point checks out with DR-G29 last and the Blueprint-readiness heading next. My own advisory is fully discharged and then some: the claim carries an inline corpus that maps one-to-one onto v5's three inputs, all three not-that-gate distinctions I asked for, and a fourth against G24 that is accurate against G24's live claim. The objection is one cell. v5's EE-7a invariant says the default useful install is core plus host plus one selected TypeScript closure plus future DR-131 pack. The proposed claim drops future, so an adopted register cell would recite the pack as a present component of the useful install while DR-131's own row is still an open hard blocker — and the draft's header expressly refuses to invent the pack, so the bytes contradict the stated intent. What persuades me it is a slip rather than a position is that the drafter was careful everywhere else: the evidence cell never requires the pack, and v5's EE-7a input tests only core-only advertisement and closure omission. I graded it SHOULD-FIX rather than MUST-FIX because membership in the selection is v5's own position and only the temporal qualifier is lost, and I note plainly that Codex may reasonably grade it higher — at D-140 and again at D-157 its harder grade was the better call. On D-157 I missed the analogous defect by reading v5's pass strings truncated; this time I read EE-7a, EE-7b and EE-7d in full, and the evidence cell does correctly cover both EE-7a limbs, EE-7b's role-list refusal and EE-7d's abandonment test.
